attacks.claim: TRAILING_PUNCT unconditionally strips a trailing ')' or ']', so a balanced URL such as a Wikipedia link ending in '(...)' is linked to a truncated address. The test only covers the stray-')' case.

The `[...]+$` replace regex is quadratic on a long punctuation run that is not at the end of the URL. The diff caps neither description length nor URL length, so a pathological description could slow every viewer's render. This only bites at very large inputs.
attacks.evidence: const raw = m[0].replace(TRAILING_PUNCT, '');  ABSENT: any description length cap or pathological-input test

attacks.claim: The PR text and test title say truncation never cuts mid-word, but the fallback hard-cuts an unbroken leading text run at the limit, and the test asserts that behavior. The behavior is reasonable but the description is inaccurate.
attacks.evidence: "truncation only cuts at whitespace or between tokens" vs expect(truncate(tokenize('x'.repeat(400)), 280)...'x'.repeat(280)

attacks.claim: A leading link is shown whole however long it is, so the collapsed view can be as long as the expanded one. A long unbroken URL can also overflow a narrow phone container because no overflow-wrap rule is added.
attacks.evidence: out.push(t); // a leading link is shown whole rather than collapsing to nothing  ABSENT: overflow-wrap/word-break rule

attacks.claim: When the cut lands before a link, the kept text retains its trailing space, so the ellipsis renders after a gap ("see …").
The limit is counted in UTF-16 units in the main path but in code points in the fallback, so the budget is inconsistent for emoji.
Links open in a new tab with no accessible indication of that, and the link text is the full raw URL.
attacks.evidence: {t.value}
